title: Keyboard Concerto No. 5 in F minor
hook: Under ten minutes long, with one of Bach’s best-loved slow songs, sung by a harpsichord over plucked strings.

painting.title: A Young Woman seated at a Virginal
painting.pairingNote: A woman plays a small keyboard instrument of the harpsichord family while a bass viol waits in the foreground; keyboard and strings together, and the quiet, inward light of the concerto’s Largo.

facts: Bach wrote this concerto out in Leipzig around 1738, as the fifth of a set of six concertos for harpsichord and strings in his own hand (the manuscript is now in the Berlin State Library). Why he gathered them is not known. One idea links them to the Collegium Musicum, the society of students and musicians he directed, which gave weekly concerts at Zimmermann’s coffee house; another to a visit to the court at Dresden in 1738.

Like most of the set, it is an arrangement of older music. The outer movements probably come from a lost violin concerto in G minor: in several places in the manuscript Bach first wrote the notes a step too high, as if copying from a G minor original, and then corrected them. Violinists today play a reconstruction of that concerto.

The slow movement has its own history. It is also the opening sinfonia of the cantata *Ich steh mit einem Fuß im Grabe* (I stand with one foot in the grave), BWV 156, first performed in 1727 or 1729, where an oboe sings the melody in F major. It probably began as the slow movement of a lost oboe concerto, and its first bars almost match the opening of a flute concerto by Bach’s friend Georg Philipp Telemann. It has been heard on its own in films, among them Woody Allen’s *Hannah and Her Sisters* (1986).

Concertos for a keyboard soloist were new. Until then the harpsichord had mostly played the [[continuo|continuo]], filling in the harmony underneath. Here it steps forward: the right hand takes the old violin or oboe part, and in the full-band passages the harpsichord plays along with everyone else.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a restless dialogue in F minor (I), a slow song over plucked strings (II), a quick, driving dance (III).

movements.heading: Allegro
movements.summary: Bach wrote no tempo here; players take it as a moderate Allegro. The strings and harpsichord open together with a firm, short theme, the [[ritornello|ritornello]], and almost at once the harpsichord breaks away to repeat the last figure on its own, like an echo. For the rest of the movement the band keeps a plain two-beat pulse while the harpsichord runs in [[triplet|triplet]]s, three notes to each beat.

mainIdeas.name: The ritornello
mainIdeas.description: a short, firm theme in F minor for the strings, with the harpsichord playing along.

mainIdeas.name: The solo line
mainIdeas.description: an almost unbroken stream of triplets in the harpsichord’s right hand, the kind of figure a violin plays.

stops.hear: The strings and harpsichord play a short, firm theme together; then the harpsichord, alone for a moment, repeats its last figure
stops.happening: The [[ritornello|ritornello]] in F minor, with the echo game between band and soloist built into it

stops.hear: The harpsichord sets off in quick groups of three, while the strings, in plain twos, put in short pieces of the theme
stops.happening: The first solo episode: three against two

stops.hear: The theme returns in the band, brighter, in a major key
stops.happening: The ritornello in a new key, probably A-flat major

stops.hear: The music turns darker and moves through several keys; the triplets in the harpsichord hardly stop, and the strings answer in short chords
stops.happening: The longest solo stretch, away from home

stops.hear: The firm opening theme is back in F minor

stops.label: Last 15 seconds
stops.hear: Band and harpsichord together for a short, firm close

notice: Tap the strings’ steady two beats, then listen to the harpsichord above them: it fits three notes into each beat. The two rhythms run side by side for most of the movement.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Trevor Pinnock plays the harpsichord and directs The English Concert, on period instruments, from the keyboard. The recording was made in London in November 1980 for his set of all of Bach’s harpsichord concertos. On the Spotify album this concerto is tracks 13–15.

movements.heading: Largo
movements.summary: The strings pluck soft chords in [[pizzicato|pizzicato]] and the harpsichord sings one long melody above them, slow and richly ornamented. A harpsichord cannot hold a note the way an oboe or a voice can, so Bach keeps the line alive with trills, turns and little runs. At the very end the music turns away from its home key and stops on an open chord, leading straight into the finale.

mainIdeas.name: The song
mainIdeas.description: a slow melody that starts on a long note and then unwinds in ornaments, high in the harpsichord.

mainIdeas.name: The accompaniment
mainIdeas.description: plucked chords in the strings, with the harpsichord’s left hand on the bass.

stops.hear: Soft plucked chords; above them the harpsichord begins a slow melody on a long note that blossoms into quick decoration
stops.happening: The song begins, in A-flat major

stops.hear: The melody keeps unwinding, with trills and small runs, never quite coming to rest
stops.happening: Bach writing out the ornaments a singer or oboist would improvise

stops.hear: The harmony darkens for a while
stops.happening: A turn to minor keys in the middle of the movement

stops.hear: The melody climbs back into its first, high register for a last long phrase
stops.happening: The song draws to a close

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: A few more bars, and the music stops on an open, unfinished-sounding chord
stops.happening: The link to F minor and the Presto

notice: Listen to how the harpsichord makes a slow tune sing: every long note is followed by quick ornaments that keep the sound from dying away.
Notice the last chord. It does not close the movement; it leaves a question that the Presto answers.

movements.heading: Presto
movements.summary: A fast finale in three short beats to the bar, back in F minor. The band’s [[ritornello|ritornello]] alternates with solo passages full of quick runs and leaping broken chords. The first movement’s echo game comes back the other way round: now the band repeats a figure while the harpsichord is silent.

mainIdeas.name: The ritornello
mainIdeas.description: a quick, insistent theme in three, for the whole band with the harpsichord.

mainIdeas.name: The solo
mainIdeas.description: fast runs and wide, leaping broken chords in the harpsichord, which on a violin would have been chords of two notes played together.

stops.hear: Band and harpsichord together, fast and insistent, three short beats to the bar
The harpsichord runs on alone; the strings drop to quiet chords
A short figure in the harpsichord, then the band repeats it while the harpsichord rests
stops.happening: The echo of the first movement, reversed

stops.hear: The harpsichord’s right hand leaps between high and low notes in broken chords, passing through brighter keys
stops.happening: The violin’s double stops, rewritten for the keyboard

stops.hear: The insistent opening theme returns in the band, in F minor

stops.label: Last 15 seconds
stops.hear: Everyone together for a short, hard close

notice: Compare the echoes with the first movement. There the harpsichord answered the band; here the band answers the harpsichord.

threads.title: Borrowed music
threads.body: A lost violin concerto, a lost oboe concerto, a church cantata and a theme by Telemann all stand behind this short piece. Bach was his own arranger, and in the Largo he made the old solo line richer for the harpsichord.

threads.title: Echoes
threads.body: In the first movement the harpsichord repeats the band’s figures; in the finale the band repeats the harpsichord’s.

threads.title: A plucked instrument that sings
threads.body: The harpsichord’s strings are plucked and its notes fade at once. In the Largo, over strings that are also plucked, Bach makes it sing with ornaments instead of held notes.
